name: Equity: Devices, Internet, and Time
title: Equity: Devices, Internet, and Time
answer: Personalized learning and AI tutoring depend on devices, reliable internet, and time to use them, and not every student has these. Because a tool that only some students can reach widens gaps rather than closing them, schools must plan for the student without internet at home. Equity means every student can actually benefit, not just that the same tool is offered to all.

sections.body: This idea is about the conditions that personalized learning quietly assumes: a device, a reliable internet connection, and time and support to use them. Many students have none of these, so a homework tool that only some can reach will widen gaps instead of closing them. The problem it solves is the gap between offering a tool to everyone and making sure everyone can benefit from it. It asks schools to treat access and support as part of the learning plan, not as an afterthought. Every personalized learning plan should say what happens for the student without internet at home.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Districts can lend devices and hotspots, and they can keep libraries and computer labs open before and after school. Some districts give class time for work that other students would otherwise do at home, and teachers should design assignments that can be completed in school when needed. The text does not give grade band differences, so the same practical steps apply across a school. Time and support matter as much as devices: a student with a quiet place to work and an adult to help will get more from any tool than a student caring for younger siblings in a crowded home. Every personalized learning plan should state what happens for the student without internet at home.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with a study of nearly 4,500 sixth graders in the Netherlands, which found that family income affected achievement directly and that classroom AI use did not change that advantage (Wang et al., 2026). The finding supports the claim that a homework tool only some students can reach will widen gaps rather than close them. The rest of the guidance, such as lending devices and hotspots, keeping libraries and labs open, and giving class time for work, is presented as practical steps rather than as research findings.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that devices and internet are necessary but not sufficient, because time and adult support matter just as much. The risk is that offering the same tool to all students looks fair while leaving some students unable to use it, which widens gaps. The decisions that stay with people are how to lend devices and hotspots, when to keep libraries and computer labs open, when to give class time for work others do at home, and how to design assignments that can be completed in school. Every personalized learning plan should say what happens for the student without internet at home. Nothing here is legal advice, and these are practice decisions for schools.
